newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine postal sale would set $25 mln investment.
newsitem.headline: Argentine postal sale would set $25 mln investment.

text.p: Argentina's postal privatization project, via a decree expected to be signed next week, fixes a 30-year concession and a minimum investment of $25 million a year, according to a draft copy of the decree.

The decree to sell state post and telecommunications firm ENCOTESA still awaits the signature of President Carlos Menem. But Reuters obtained a copy of the document Friday setting the parameters for eventual bidders.
It requires minimum assets of $100,000 and the technical support of an official post office of a member country of the Universal Postal Union, either as a partner or subcontractor.

The document sets a requirement of $10 million in initial capital and rules that the technical operator must, as well as being an official Postal Union member, have 50 percent higher operating volume and average productivity, as measured by items processed per employee, than ENCOTESA.
The eventual concessionaire would have freedom to set tariffs except for normal letters of up to 20g, telegrams of up to 20 words and commissions for money orders up to $1,000.
The tariff for normal letters up to 20g is set, on advice from consultancy Coopers & Lybrand, at $0.75 falling by $0.05 a year until 2002 when it would reach $0.50.
"As for money orders and simple telegrams, the tariff set by the concessionaire may not exceed the prices charged by ENCOTESA at the time of handover," reads the document.
But the draft decree allows for a cost-related tariff adjustment program to be agreed with authorities from 2003 and adjustments in the case of tax hikes directly affecting the concessionaire.

The sale of ENCOTESA has become a political hot potato because of former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo's charges that crime syndicates with links to officialdom are attempting to monopolize the postal service for criminal purposes.
Cavallo has pointed the finger at Alfredo Yabran, who has interests in the deregulated postal sector and is accused by Cavallo of being the "mafia boss" of Argentina.

In recent days, Yabran has emerged from his preferrred media silence to deny the charges and say he is in fact pulling out of the postal business and now owns only 10 percent of private postal firm ENCOTESA.

But he has also promised to fight any attempt to exclude him from the privatization, drawing an assurance from Economy Minister Roque Fernandez that the decree has "no anti-Yabran clause but neither is there a pro-Yabran clause." That provoked charges from Cavallo that the state was aiding Yabran.
The opposition Radical Party has filed suit trying to block the postal privatization decree, which it says would be a "flagrant transgression" of law and parliamentary rights.
